units.text: The ocean is changing, and these changes have important implications for all life on Earth. Scientists need to know where these changes are occurring and how fast. That's why we have the Ocean Observatories Initiative, or OOI. OOI is a science-driven ocean-observing network that delivers real-time data to researchers investigating our changing ocean on a coastal and planetary scale. Funded by the National Science Foundation, OOI data are freely available online to anyone with an internet connection. Now in its eighth year, OOI makes it possible to investigate short-lived events as well as multi-year trends. That provides researchers around the globe with critical insights into climate change and its effect on marine ecosystems.

systems. With OOI data, they can track changes in fisheries, ocean acidification, and the potential of the ocean to recycle even more carbon. OOI consists of five arrays that continuously collect ocean data with instrumented moorings, linked to shore via satellite. Two global arrays address planetary scale changes in the Irminger Sea and Gulf of Alaska.
An additional cable array wires a region of the northeast Pacific Ocean with a high-power high-speed fiber optic grid that enables observation of the seafloor and water column.
Located over an active tectonic plate, this array provides a window into hydrothermal vents and an active undersea volcano.

Gliders fill in gaps between the arrays, traveling on a data mules send oceanographic measurements back to OOI servers when they surface. The Ocean Observatories Initiative has revolutionized marine research with free access to high quality data from remote locations and at unprecedented timescales.
The only question left to answer is, how will you use OOI?
